title: Monica's tears
hook: a mother prays for years for her wayward son, Augustine, and a bishop tells her such tears won't be lost

segments.voice: Yesterday, saint: in Paul's letters, every believer; later, holy lives remembered. Your line was ordinary people, made holy. Thirteen weeks on the path.

Some love keeps people up at night: loving someone who keeps making the choice you were afraid of. Rehearsing the conversation. Trying again, and watching it go badly again. Roman North Africa. A woman named Monica has a son who is brilliant, charming, ambitious and restless. His name is Augustine. He drifts from the faith she raised him in, throws himself into success, and into a way of life that breaks her heart. She weeps for him, prays for him, follows him around. Years go by. All of this survives because, years later, Augustine told the story himself, in a book addressed to God called the Confessions. And he doesn't spare himself.
screen: `AWAKE AT NIGHT.` → `A BRILLIANT, RESTLESS SON.` → `HE TOLD IT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: At one point, Monica goes to a bishop and begs him to talk sense into her son. The bishop says no. He's not ready; leave him alone and keep praying; he'll find his own way. She won't take no. She keeps pleading, in floods of tears, until the bishop, a bit worn out, says: go your way, it cannot be that the son of these tears should perish. Augustine says his mother took that as if it had sounded from heaven. It didn't fix anything quickly. When Augustine decided to sail for Rome, he lied to her to slip away, and left her weeping on the shore. So she followed him, across the sea, all the way to Milan. There, finally, the road turned. Augustine was baptized at Easter by the bishop of Milan, Ambrose. Not long after, mother and son stood at a window in the port town of Ostia, near Rome, talking quietly about God, and Augustine describes the two of them touching something eternal for a moment. A few days later she fell ill and died, far from home, content. The son of those tears became a writer whom Christians in many churches still read, and churches honor Monica as a saint. Christians have held on to her story for the plainest reason: it says that years of tears, poured out for someone who seems not to be listening, are not wasted.
screen: `THE BISHOP SAYS NO.` · `THE SON OF THESE TEARS.` · `SHE FOLLOWS HIM TO MILAN.` · `A WINDOW AT OSTIA.` · then, large: `TEARS ARE NOT WASTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've worried over for a long time, who never calls back, or keeps choosing what hurts them, and let yourself feel it, even if tears come. If you pray, bring them to God in whatever words you have, or none; if you don't, hold them in your mind with love, the way Monica did. Don't try to fix them; just don't let go.
Monica's tears. A mother's long, stubborn love, and a bishop's promise. This week: Athens, a shipwreck, an epistle, Philemon, agape, saint, and Monica.
Your line: tears are not wasted. Tomorrow, her son hears a child's voice in a garden. Rest easy tonight.

howItsDone: Saint Monica is honored as a patron of mothers and of those who pray for loved ones who have drifted from faith. In the Catholic calendar her feast is August 27, the day before Saint Augustine's.

myth: the bishop agreed at once to talk to Augustine
he refused, and told her to keep praying. only her tears got the famous promise out of him.
Augustine slipped away to Rome by lying to his mother
he tells it himself in the Confessions, and she followed him anyway.
Monica died before Augustine was baptized
he was baptized at Easter; she died soon after, at Ostia.

fork.setup: you're Monica. a bishop has just told you to leave your son alone and keep praying. what do you do?
options: go and confront your son yourself.
fork.reveal: she keeps pressing, weeping, until the bishop says: go your way, it cannot be that the son of these tears should perish.

original.note: Latin: the son of these tears, from the bishop's words in Augustine's Confessions 3.12.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pious mother in a painting.
what it means: a real woman who wept, pleaded, got lied to, crossed a sea, and would not stop loving her son.
what a scholar hears: we know her almost entirely through her son's Confessions (books 3, 5 and 9), a life story written in Latin as a prayer to God.
